title: Mooncakes Sell Only Two Months a Year, Yet Build a 28.2 Billion Yuan Business
dek: Bound to Mid-Autumn Festival, mooncakes are trapped in a narrow sales window — but the 28.2 billion yuan scale comes from gifting scenarios and flexible custom production lines, not from flavor innovation.
why: Worth listening for food industry practitioners and anyone wanting to understand holiday consumption businesses, but information density is low — much of the runtime is spent on faction taxonomy and flavors, with the business mechanics concentrated in the middle and later sections.
who: Food industry founders, brands doing corporate custom gifts, and investors wanting to understand the logic of holiday consumption businesses.
skip: 0:12-2:03 Personal taste preferences and Taiwan date paste pastry — unrelated to business analysis.

points.h: Zongzi can sell year-round, mooncakes cannot
points.body: Zongzi is tied to Dragon Boat Festival, but once vacuum-sealed for long shelf life it can sell all year, and Wufangzhai (五芳斋) even opened restaurants to put zongzi into everyday scenarios. Mooncakes' problem isn't that the craft can't achieve long shelf life — it's that they're defined as "traditional festival pastries mainly eaten during Mid-Autumn Festival," and the national standard GB19855 writes the season directly into the definition. So of two festival foods, zongzi can decouple from the holiday through shelf life and channels, while mooncakes cannot.

points.h: The national standard draws hard lines on fillings
points.body: Lotus paste mooncakes must contain at least 60% lotus seeds, fruit mooncakes must contain at least 25% fruit products, and five-kernel mooncakes must use exactly five nuts: walnut, almond, olive kernel, melon seed, and sesame. The purpose of these lines is to push up ingredient costs and prevent cheap candied winter melon, red-and-green shreds, and low-grade nuts from being used as filler. For consumers, reading the order of ingredients on the label is enough to judge how much of what is actually in there.

points.h: Why custard lava mooncakes are made so small
points.body: Custard lava mooncakes are small not out of stinginess but because of structure. The outside is flaky pastry, the middle is a custard layer, and the innermost is the lava layer — the custard layer acts as a moisture barrier. Production requires two rounds of baking to keep the lava semi-solid, and the lava's melting point must be engineered: solid during transport, then a few seconds in the microwave turns it into flowing liquid. If heated too long, the lava gets absorbed by the pastry and it reverts to an ordinary custard mooncake.

points.h: Five preconditions for "everything can be a mooncake"
points.body: Not everything can be stuffed into a mooncake. First is water content — hot-and-sour soup mooncakes are impossible because there's too much water to contain. Second is safety — meat, egg, and dairy are also favored by microbes, so processing temperatures and sterilization processes must be tested repeatedly. Third is particle size — too large and the pastry can't hold it, too fine and you can't taste it. Fourth is flavor retention after high-temperature baking — some aromas simply disappear once baked. Fifth is whether the cost can be handled. So long-term stable flavors are ones confirmed by generation after generation.

points.h: Choosing an OEM factory isn't about picking the biggest
points.body: When big brands make branded mooncakes through OEM, there's a common misconception: you must choose the best OEM factory in the country. But a top-tier OEM's production scale actually doesn't match yours. Indicators you can screen on include registered capital, tax payment records, number of employees with social insurance contributions, and accumulated days without safety incidents. Also, the nine major factions correspond to different factories — you can't ask Guangzhou Restaurant (广州酒家) to produce Shanxi egg-skin mooncakes; they simply don't have that capability or production line.

points.h: Flexible lines can take orders of a few hundred boxes
points.body: Mooncake production is semi-automated and semi-manual — wrapping and forming machines can do their part, but brushing egg wash, pressing patterns, and stamping require human hands, which actually makes it favorable for OEM and customization. Flexible factories can go as small as a few hundred boxes, and can do thousands or tens of thousands of boxes too. If a company has only 50 employees, it can use the factory's existing mooncakes directly and only needs to design the gift box. This small-batch, fast-response capability is the core of why mooncakes can support a corporate customization business.

points.h: The 28.2 billion yuan scale is propped up by gifting
points.body: In 2025, China's mooncake output was 518,000 tons and sales reached 28.2 billion RMB, both down from the previous year. At 80 grams each that's about 6.4 billion pieces; at 100 grams, about 5.18 billion pieces — across a population of 1.4 billion, an average of three to four per person. For comparison, Dragon Boat Festival zongzi annual sales are about 10 to 11 billion yuan, and instant noodles about 68 to 120 billion yuan. That mooncakes can do 28.2 billion yuan selling only two months a year comes down to their gifting attribute — brands prepare large volumes of PR gifts at the two annual nodes of Chinese New Year and Mid-Autumn Festival, and zongzi's gifting attribute is far weaker than mooncakes'.

points.h: 499 yuan is a number forced out by the regulatory line
points.body: In 2022, the National Development and Reform Commission and three other departments jointly issued an announcement implementing key oversight on boxed mooncakes priced above 500 yuan per unit. So the highest mooncake price on the market is 499. The calculation logic: a box of mooncakes costs about 70 yuan per box, and adding channel commissions and allocated expenses, it can't exceed 500 yuan. Back when the economy was good there were sky-high mooncakes with very expensive tea or liquor bundled in, even wooden gift boxes, with both cost and price very high.

points.h: Mini package is becoming a trend
points.body: In the food industry these past two years there's a clear trend called mini package — packaging made smaller. On one hand, it can be finished in one sitting after opening; on the other, consumers just want a quick treat and don't want to eat that much, and small packaging also lets them buy many flavors at once. Mooncakes are moving in this direction too, because it's hard for one person to finish a whole mooncake — usually it's cut into several pieces to share. Made smaller, one person can at least finish one, and waste is reduced.

points.h: New flavors die before reaching consumers
points.body: Brands launch five new flavors each year to see which gets eliminated, but a flavor having no repeat purchase doesn't necessarily mean consumers dislike it — it may simply never have reached consumers. Because most mooncakes are gifts, constantly being regifted and circulated, the recipient never eats it and passes it on. So next year they won't want to buy that flavor either, because this year they never tasted it. Brands with physical stores have an advantage: they can do tastings, letting consumers try before deciding.
